docs.title: Adding Knowledge to LLMs
docs.text:
A self-paced, hands-on workshop. You'll take a general-purpose LLM, teach it the products, policies and safety rules of a company it has never heard of, and make it small enough to deploy.

Every lab runs in Google Colab: nothing to install and no GPU of your own. The free T4 GPU covers the whole core path. Colab Pro unlocks bonus exercises with bigger models.

docs.text: Progress is saved in this browser only.

docs.title: Meet Lumora Energy
docs.text:
All five modules follow one company: Lumora Energy. It's fictional, invented for this workshop, so no model has ever seen anything about it. That makes it a clean test: whatever the model knows about Lumora at the end, you taught it.

Lumora was founded in 2017 in Rotterdam and makes home energy storage, sold through certified installers in nine European countries:

Product What it is Vault 10 A wall-mounted home battery: 10.2 kWh, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, 98 kg Vault 15 The larger, floor-mounted model: 15.4 kWh, 141 kg Bridge A 10 kW hybrid inverter that connects solar panels, Vault batteries and the grid Lumora Home The companion app for owners: live energy data, operating modes, warranty claims

Around the products sit the documents any company has: a 12-year warranty, a returns policy, error codes such as E-204 and E-317, installer certification rules, a safety protocol, and staff policies that a customer assistant should never quote.

docs.title: The job: build Lumora's support assistant
docs.text:
Lumora wants an assistant that answers customer questions correctly, in Lumora's friendly voice, and that never gives unsafe advice about a 10 kWh battery. Ask a general model today and it either guesses or says it doesn't know:

A customer asks The right answer What a general model typically does What's the usable capacity of the Vault 10? 10.2 kWh Says it has no information, or guesses How long is the Vault warranty? 12 years Guesses a typical number What does error E-204 mean? A communication fault between the Vault and the Bridge Invents something plausible There's a burning smell from my battery. What do I do? Keep away, leave the building and call 112, then contact Lumora Support Lists possible causes to investigate

The last row is the dangerous one. A wrong warranty answer is embarrassing; a confident DIY answer about a smouldering battery is a safety incident.

docs.title: What you'll do, module by module
docs.text:
Each module solves the next problem on the way to that assistant, and each one builds on the previous module's output.

flowchart LR
  A["Lumora's raw<br/>documents"] -->|"M1 curate"| B["Clean corpus<br/>+ Q&A pairs"]
  B -->|"M2 measure"| C["Test set<br/>+ trusted judge"]
  C -->|"M3 teach"| D["Model that knows<br/>Lumora"]
  D -->|"M4 shrink"| E["Smaller,<br/>faster model"]
  E -->|"M5 make safe"| F["Safety-aligned<br/>assistant"]

docs.title: 1. Curate Lumora's data
docs.text:
Lumora's problem: the documents are a mess. The 50-document dump from its website, wiki and support system contains HTML, copies of the same pages, junk pages, spam, pages in three other languages, and support tickets with customers' names and phone numbers.

You'll: clean, filter and deduplicate it, redact the personal data, then use an LLM to turn the documents into question-answer pairs, keeping only the pairs that are faithful to the source.

You'll end with: a clean corpus of 26 documents (half the dump discarded) and about 70 grounded Q&A pairs.

docs.title: 2. Measure what the model knows
docs.text:
Lumora's problem: before teaching the model anything, you need a fair way to tell whether it worked. "It seems better" isn't evidence.

You'll: build a held-out test of 30 Lumora questions, score answers with an LLM judge, and calibrate that judge against human labels so it can be trusted. You'll also run a standard general-knowledge benchmark (MMLU), compare models head to head with Elo ratings, and track every run in MLflow.

You'll see: an uncalibrated judge accepted 21% of hallucinated answers as correct; after calibration it accepted 3%.

docs.title: 3. Teach the model about Lumora
docs.text:
Lumora's problem: the base model doesn't know the facts, doesn't answer in a helpful question-and-answer format, and doesn't sound like Lumora.

You'll: use three techniques, each for a different job:

  • Continued pretraining on the curated documents, to teach the facts
  • Supervised fine-tuning on the Q&A pairs, to teach it to answer questions
  • Preference alignment (DPO), to give it Lumora's warm, casual voice

You'll see: on the 30 held-out questions, the base model answered 10% correctly; after continued pretraining and fine-tuning, 70%. Its general knowledge (MMLU) stayed level.

docs.title: 4. Make it small enough to deploy
docs.text:
Lumora's problem: the assistant has to run cheaply and quickly for thousands of customers.

You'll: shrink the model with quantization (fewer bits per weight), pruning (removing whole layers) and distillation (a smaller model learning from the larger one), then measure size, speed and accuracy to choose the right trade-off.

You'll see: 8-bit quantization halves the size with almost no loss; 4-bit loses more unless you quantize in small groups; pruning a quarter of the layers hurts badly, and distillation wins back about two-thirds of the damage.

docs.title: 5. Assessment: make it safe
docs.text:
Lumora's problem: when a customer reports smoke, swelling or a hissing battery, or asks how to open the Vault, the assistant must follow Lumora's safety protocol every time, without becoming so cautious that it refuses ordinary questions.

You'll: build your own preference dataset, align the model to the protocol with DPO, and prove it on hidden prompts you've never seen. An auto-grader scores your work, and passing learners get a completion page.

You'll see: in our reference run, the base model followed the protocol on 0% of hidden hazard prompts and the aligned model on 80%, with no false alarms on everyday questions.

About the numbers

The results above come from our own reference runs on the free-track models (Qwen2.5, 0.5B-1.5B parameters). Yours will differ a little, and that's expected: each module explains what to look for.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
\"Cannot connect to GPU backend\" / no T4 available

Free GPUs are shared and can run out at peak times. Options: retry in 30-60 minutes, run on CPU (the notebook switches to tiny models automatically; generation is slower), or use Colab Pro.

CUDA out of memory

Runtime -> Restart session, then re-run from the top. Lower batch_size in the generation cell. Make sure you didn't load two models at once (del gen; import gc, torch; gc.collect(); torch.cuda.empty_cache()).

git clone fails in the setup cell

Check that the REPO_URL in the first cell points at the course repository and that it is public.

Setup says \"⚠ Restart to reload dependencies\"

You can ignore this message from spaCy in the Module 1 setup cell. The notebook loads the model in a way that works without a restart. Restart only if a later cell fails with E050 (below).

OSError: [E050] Can't find model 'en_core_web_sm'

The spaCy model didn't finish downloading. Run !python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm, then Runtime -> Restart session and re-run the setup cells.

My check says FAIL but I think my code is right

Read the hint: line and print the intermediate DataFrame. Checks compare against an answer key built into the dataset (data/raw/answer_key.json). If you're sure it's a bug, set USE_SOLUTIONS = True to continue and open an issue on the course repo.

I lost my outputs when Colab disconnected

Set USE_DRIVE = True in the setup cell so everything is saved to Google Drive.

Hugging Face 401 / 403 when loading a model

The labs' Qwen models don't need a token. If you swapped in a gated model (e.g. Llama), accept its licence on its model page, add HF_TOKEN in Colab Secrets, and enable Notebook access for it. Approval can take a few minutes.

Out of memory during training (Modules 3-5)

The labs are sized for a 16 GB T4. If you hit an out-of-memory error: Runtime -> Restart session, make sure no other notebook is running in the same session, and re-run from the top. You can also halve per_device_train_batch_size and double gradient_accumulation_steps: the effective batch stays the same and memory drops.

Assessment pairs or model disappeared

Set USE_DRIVE = True in the Module 5 setup cell. Pairs are saved to MyDrive/llm-knowledge-workshop/m05/preference_pairs.jsonl and reloaded automatically. Delete the file to rebuild.

docs.title: Module 1: Data curation & synthetic data generation
docs.text: Time: about 75 minutes, reading and lab together  |  Track: Free (T4), with a Pro bonus

docs.title: The situation
docs.text:
Lumora Energy, the home-battery company in this workshop's case study, wants an assistant that answers questions about its products: the Vault batteries, the Bridge inverter and the Lumora Home app. A general model knows nothing about them. Later modules teach it, but every one of those methods learns from data, so this module builds that data.

Lumora has handed you a dump of 50 documents pulled from its website, internal wiki and support system. As in any real company, it's a mess:

What's in the dump How many Useful product, policy and support documents 20 Exact copies of some of those documents 5 Lightly edited copies (a footer added, a line changed) 5 Raw HTML copies of web pages, with scripts and menus 5 Junk: a 404 page, a login prompt, a cookie banner, a blank page 4 Keyword spam 2 Pages in German, Spanish and Dutch 3 Support tickets containing customer names, emails and phone numbers 6

By the end of the module you'll have turned it into the two kinds of data that Module 3 trains on:

  1. A curated corpus: clean, unique documents with no personal data. Module 3 uses it for continued pretraining, which teaches the model Lumora's facts.
  2. A set of question-answer pairs generated from those documents. Module 3 uses it for supervised fine-tuning, which teaches the model to answer questions.

Module 3 ships a larger version of both, built with this same pipeline, so it works even if you skip ahead; you can swap in your own files from this lab.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Every training method in this workshop does the same thing: it makes the model more likely to produce text that looks like its training data. The model can't tell which parts you meant it to learn. Leave the dump as it is and here's what it learns:

Left in the data What the model learns The same page five times To recite that page word for word, at the expense of everything else Cookie banners and menus To say "Accept all cookies?" in the middle of an answer Customer emails and phone numbers To repeat them when prompted: a privacy incident German and Dutch pages To switch language at random

Research backs this up. Deduplicating training data cut word-for-word memorisation roughly tenfold (Lee et al., 2022). Heavily filtered web data trains better models than larger unfiltered data (Hugging Face's FineWeb, 2024). And personal data that goes into a model can be pulled back out: researchers extracted names, phone numbers and emails from GPT-2 (Carlini et al., 2021). Curation is where you decide what the model knows.

docs.title: The plan: a funnel
docs.text:
A good pipeline is a funnel. Cheap, fast steps remove most of the junk first, so slower steps only handle what's left. This module follows the funnel from top to bottom:

flowchart TB
  subgraph A["Part A: curate the documents"]
    direction LR
    R[Raw dump<br/>50 docs] --> C[2. Clean] --> F[3. Filter junk] --> D[4. Remove<br/>duplicates] --> P[5. Redact<br/>personal data] --> O[Curated corpus<br/>26 docs]
  end
  subgraph B["Part B: turn them into training examples"]
    direction LR
    G[6. Generate<br/>Q&A pairs] --> V[7. Keep only<br/>faithful pairs] --> Q[Q&A set]
  end
  A --> B

Part A (steps 1-5) curates the documents; Step 1 is looking at the raw data. Part B (steps 6-7) turns the curated documents into training examples.

Open the lab now and work through it alongside this page

The notebook uses the same step numbers as this page. Each step below ends with a ▶ Lab box that tells you which exercise to do. Every exercise has an automatic check.

Exercise Step The check confirms 1. clean_text 2 6 unit tests pass 2. Quality filters 3 junk, spam and foreign pages removed; all good documents kept 3. Deduplication 4 exactly 20 unique knowledge documents remain 4. PII redaction 5 no emails, phones or names left; error codes kept 5. Synthetic Q&A 6-7 at least 20 pairs, all grounded in their source Pro bonus 7 LLM-as-a-judge filtering (Colab Pro only)

docs.title: Step 1: Look at the raw data
docs.text:
Before writing a single rule, look at the data. Every rule in a real pipeline should trace back to a problem someone saw. Rules written without looking remove good data and miss bad data.

▶ Lab: Step 1

Run the setup cells, then scroll through the raw table. Try to spot each problem from the table above: the HTML, the copies, the junk pages, the foreign languages and the customer details. Which would hurt the model most if left in?

The first thing you'll notice is that many documents are mostly not text: they're HTML. That's the first job.

docs.title: Step 2: Clean the text
docs.text:
A scraped product page is mostly tags, scripts, menus, cookie notices and footers wrapped around a few paragraphs of real content. Cleaning extracts the content:

  1. Remove <script> and <style> blocks, including their contents. Removing only the tags leaves raw JavaScript in your training data.
  2. Strip the remaining tags, keeping line breaks so later rules can work line by line.
  3. Decode HTML entities: & becomes &, < becomes <.
  4. Normalise unicode. There are many ways to write "the same" character: non-breaking spaces, full-width digits, zero-width characters. NFKC normalisation maps them to one standard form, so "10.2 kWh" with an odd space is treated like normal text.
  5. Remove boilerplate lines such as menus, footers and "Subscribe to our newsletter". The lab uses simple line patterns. Production tools such as trafilatura use page layout and text density instead.
  6. Collapse repeated whitespace.

▶ Lab: Exercise 1, write clean_text

Implement the six steps, run the check, and compare a document before and after cleaning.

Clean text shows the next problem clearly: some documents have no useful content at all.

docs.title: Step 3: Filter out junk
docs.text:
With the HTML gone, you can judge documents by their text. Large pretraining projects publish their filter rules, and they're surprisingly simple. DeepMind's Gopher rules (Rae et al., 2021) and Google's C4 rules (Raffel et al., 2020) include:

Rule Catches Example threshold Word count Empty pages, "404", cookie notices Keep 50-100,000 words (Gopher) Mean word length Gibberish, minified code 3-10 characters Symbol-to-word ratio Hashtag spam, code dumps Under 0.1 for # or ... Stopword presence Tables, lists, keyword spam At least 2 common English words Repeated lines or word pairs Templated spam Top 2-gram covers under 20% of text Lines ending in punctuation Menus, fragments C4 keeps only such lines

Lumora's documents are short, so the lab uses three rules sized for them:

Rule Removes from the Lumora dump Word count of at least 20 The 404 page, login prompt, cookie banner and blank page Unique-word ratio of at least 0.35 (unique words ÷ total words) The keyword spam, which scores around 0.05 Language ID: langdetect says English with probability of at least 0.9 The German, Spanish and Dutch pages Why use a language identifier instead of checking for English words?

Checking for common English words sounds simpler, but it fails on short texts. A Dutch sentence like "Lumora Energy is in 2017 opgericht in Rotterdam" contains the English words "is" and "in", and can score higher than a short English support ticket. A trained language identifier looks at character patterns across the whole text and is far more reliable. NeMo Curator uses fastText's language-ID model, which covers 176 languages.

▶ Lab: Exercise 2, write quality_filter

Implement the three rules. The check confirms every junk, spam and foreign page is removed and every good document is kept. Removing good data is a failure too.

Beyond the lab: model-based filters

Rules can tell that a page is short or repetitive, but not whether it's informative. Large pipelines add a learned filter after the rules:

  • Perplexity filtering (CCNet): a small language model trained on high-quality text, such as Wikipedia, scores each document, and text it finds very surprising is dropped.
  • Quality classifiers: a strong LLM rates a sample of documents (for example "educational value 0-5"), a small fast classifier learns from those ratings, and then it scores billions of documents. FineWeb-Edu was built this way.
  • LLM judges: the most accurate and most expensive option, so used last on small sets. You'll use one in Step 7 to judge Q&A pairs.

Lumora's 50 documents don't need this, which is why it isn't in the funnel above.

What's left is all real content, but much of it is the same content more than once.

docs.title: Why duplicates hurt
docs.text:
A document that appears five times gets five times the training. The model memorises it at the expense of everything else, wastes compute, and becomes more likely to repeat it word for word. Duplicates also make evaluation unreliable when test questions leak into training data, a problem you'll meet again in Modules 2 and 3.

The Lumora dump has three kinds of copy, and they need two techniques.

docs.title: Exact copies: hashing
docs.text: Turn each document into a hash, a short fingerprint of its text (the lab uses MD5 of the lower-cased text), and keep one document per fingerprint. It's fast and certain, but it only catches identical text: change a single character and the fingerprint is completely different.

docs.title: Near copies: MinHash
docs.text:
Lumora's edited copies and HTML mirrors aren't identical, so hashing misses them. To catch them you need a measure of how similar two documents are, and a way to compute it quickly.

  1. Turn each document into a set of shingles. A shingle is a run of consecutive words; the lab uses 5. "The Vault 10 weighs 98 kg" gives {"the vault 10 weighs 98", "vault 10 weighs 98 kg"}. Near copies share most of their shingles.
  2. Measure the overlap with Jaccard similarity: the number of shingles two documents share, divided by the number of distinct shingles they have between them. Identical documents score 1.0, a copy with one sentence added scores about 0.85, and unrelated documents score close to 0.
  3. Estimate it cheaply with MinHash. Comparing full shingle sets is slow, so MinHash shrinks every document to a fixed signature of 128 numbers. The fraction of positions where two signatures match estimates their Jaccard similarity.
  4. Avoid comparing every pair with LSH. Locality-sensitive hashing sorts signatures into buckets so that only likely-similar documents are compared at all.
How it works: the maths behind MinHash and LSH

Jaccard similarity of shingle sets \(A\) and \(B\):

\[J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\]

MinHash applies a random hash function \(h\) to every shingle and keeps only the minimum value. The key property is:

\[P\big[\min h(A) = \min h(B)\big] = J(A, B)\]

The chance that two documents share a MinHash value equals their Jaccard similarity. Repeat with 128 different hash functions and the fraction of matches estimates \(J\) closely, whatever the documents' length.

LSH. Comparing every pair of signatures is still \(O(n^2)\): about 500 billion comparisons for a million documents. LSH splits each signature into \(b\) bands of \(r\) rows and hashes each band into a bucket. Documents that share a bucket in any band become candidate pairs. A pair with similarity \(s\) becomes a candidate with probability

\[P(\text{candidate}) = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b\]

This is an S-shaped curve: pairs above the threshold almost always collide, and pairs well below almost never do. datasketch picks \(b\) and \(r\) for you from the threshold you give it. Chapter 3 of the free book Mining of Massive Datasets (in Further reading) explains this step by step.

docs.title: Choosing the threshold
docs.text:
The similarity threshold decides what counts as a duplicate, and it's a trade-off:

Threshold Effect Risk High (0.95) Only near-identical copies removed Edited copies and HTML mirrors slip through Medium (0.7) Catches edited copies and HTML mirrors Lab default Low (0.3) Very aggressive Different documents that share boilerplate get merged

▶ Lab: Exercise 3, write exact_dedup and fuzzy_dedup

The check enforces both sides of the trade-off: no duplicated content left, and exactly 20 unique knowledge documents kept. Then try thresholds of 0.3 and 0.95 and see what goes wrong at each extreme.

Beyond the lab: semantic deduplication

MinHash finds documents that share words. Two documents that say the same thing in different words have low Jaccard similarity. Semantic deduplication (for example SemDeDup) turns each document into an embedding, groups similar ones, and removes items that are very close together. NeMo Curator supports exact, fuzzy and semantic deduplication on GPU.

The corpus is now clean and unique. One problem is left, and it's the riskiest: the support tickets contain real customers' details.

docs.title: What counts as personal data
docs.text:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is anything that identifies a person: names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, account numbers, and sometimes combinations of harmless-looking details. Laws such as GDPR restrict how it may be processed, and a model that memorises it can leak it.

The support tickets are worth keeping: they show how customers describe problems. So rather than delete them, you redact them, replacing the personal details and keeping the rest.

docs.title: How Presidio finds it
docs.text:
Microsoft Presidio combines several detectors and gives each finding a confidence score:

Detector Finds Example Named-entity recognition (a spaCy model) Names, places, organisations "Maria Jansen" is a PERSON Patterns with validation Structured identifiers Emails; phone numbers checked with phonenumbers Context words Raises confidence "call me on ..." makes a nearby number more likely to be a phone number

You then choose what to replace each finding with:

Option Output Use when Replace <PERSON> Training data: keeps the sentence shape, removes the identity (lab choice) Mask M**** J***** Showing records to people Hash a91f3c... You need to link records without revealing who they are Fake replacement "Anna Smith" You want natural-looking text (keep it consistent)

docs.title: Don't redact too much
docs.text:
Redaction is a trade-off between missing personal data (a privacy risk) and redacting things that aren't personal (destroying knowledge). Turn on every entity type and Presidio may tag "E-204" or "24 months" as an identifier or a date, and those are exactly the facts the model should learn. The lab limits detection to PERSON, EMAIL_ADDRESS and PHONE_NUMBER.

▶ Lab: Exercise 4, redact the support tickets

The check confirms that no emails, phone numbers or names remain, and that error codes such as E-204 survive.

Small models miss things

The lab uses spaCy's small English model, which is fast but imperfect. Names in unusual formats, or from languages it rarely saw, can slip through. Production pipelines use larger models, extra patterns for their own data, and spot checks by people.

docs.title: Part A result
docs.text:
Here's what the funnel did to Lumora's dump:

Step Documents left Removed Raw dump 50 After filtering junk 41 4 junk, 2 spam, 3 foreign-language After exact deduplication 36 5 exact copies After near-duplicate removal 26 5 edited copies, 5 HTML mirrors After redaction 26 none removed; 6 tickets redacted Curated corpus 26 48% of the dump discarded

Throwing away half the raw data is normal; large web pipelines discard far more. The notebook saves this corpus as curated_corpus.jsonl.

docs.title: Part B: Turn the documents into training examples
Why generate data?
docs.text: The curated corpus teaches the model facts. But Lumora wants an assistant that answers questions, and for that the model needs examples of questions paired with good answers. Nobody at Lumora has written those, and writing thousands by hand is slow and expensive. A capable LLM can turn documents into question-answer pairs in minutes. This is called synthetic data.

docs.title: Common approaches
docs.text:
Approach How it works Used for Grounded generation Give the LLM a source document and ask for Q&A pairs about it Domain knowledge (this lab) Self-Instruct Start from seed tasks; the LLM writes new tasks and answers; filter; repeat General instruction data Evol-Instruct The LLM rewrites instructions to be harder or more varied Complex reasoning data Persona-driven Ask the same thing as different kinds of user Variety Distillation A strong "teacher" model answers prompts for a smaller "student" Transferring ability (Module 4)

The lab uses grounded generation: the model reads each knowledge document (not the support tickets) and writes four question-answer pairs about specific facts in it.

▶ Lab: Exercise 5, part 1: generate candidates

Read the generation prompt, run it over the knowledge documents, and look at a few of the candidate pairs it produces.

Read a few candidates and you'll see why the next step exists: some answers sound right but aren't in the document.

docs.title: What can go wrong with synthetic data
docs.text: Risk What it looks like What to do Hallucination The answer states a fact the document doesn't contain Grounding filter, LLM judge Low variety 80 versions of "What is X?" Ask for varied question types; remove duplicate questions Format errors Missing question marks, two pairs merged into one Parse and validate the format Model collapse Models trained on model output, generation after generation, get worse (Shumailov et al., 2024) Keep real data in the mix; check synthetic data Licence terms Some model licences restrict using their output to train other models Check the generator's terms

docs.title: The grounding filter
docs.text:
For each generated answer, take its content words (dropping "the", "is" and other common words) and measure what fraction also appear in the source document:

\[\text{overlap} = \frac{|\text{content}(\text{answer}) \cap \text{content}(\text{document})|}{|\text{content}(\text{answer})|}\]

Keep the pair if the overlap is at least 0.6. It's crude, since a paraphrase may use different words, but it reliably catches answers that bring in facts from nowhere, such as "Anyone who has observed unusual conditions should check for ventilation gaps" when the document says nothing about it.

▶ Lab: Exercise 5, part 2: write the grounding filter

Implement is_grounded, drop duplicate questions, and run the check. Look at the rejected pairs: would you want the model to learn them?

docs.title: When word overlap isn't enough
docs.text:
Word overlap can't check that an answer is correct. "The warranty is 15 years" overlaps well with a document that says "12-year warranty". Catching that needs a model that reads the document and the answer together: an LLM judge.

▶ Lab: Pro bonus, LLM-as-a-judge (Colab Pro only)

On an L4 or A100 runtime, a 7B model grades each pair from 1 to 5 for faithfulness, and you keep only pairs scored 4 or 5. On the free T4 the notebook skips this cell. Module 2 spends a whole section on making judges like this trustworthy.

The notebook saves the Q&A set as sft_qa.jsonl.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Look at the data first. Every rule in this module came from a problem visible in the raw table.
  • Cheap steps first, expensive steps last. Rules and hashing remove most of the junk for almost no compute; LLMs only see what survives.
  • Every filter is a trade-off. Too strict and you lose good data; too loose and junk gets through. The checks in this lab test both sides.
  • Synthetic data needs checking. Generating pairs is easy; making sure they're faithful to the source is the real work.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Writing filters without looking at the data first
  • Removing <script> tags but leaving the code inside them
  • Removing only exact copies, so edited copies and HTML mirrors survive
  • Never tuning the deduplication threshold
  • Redacting every entity type, so error codes and numbers disappear
  • Trusting synthetic data without checking it against the source
  • Not recording what each step removed, so you can't explain or reproduce the dataset

docs.title: Module 2: Evaluating LLMs
docs.text: Time: about 85 minutes, reading and lab together  |  Track: Free (T4), with a Pro bonus

docs.title: The situation
docs.text:
In Module 1 you built Lumora's training data. Before anyone spends GPU budget training a model on it (Module 3), Lumora's leadership asks two questions:

  1. How good are the candidate models in general?
  2. How much do they already know about our products?

They want numbers they can trust, and a record of every experiment so that Module 3's trained models can be compared against exactly the same baseline.

The candidates are two open models of different sizes: on the free track, Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen2.5-1.5B (on Pro, 1.5B and 7B). By the end of this module you'll have:

  • their general-knowledge scores on a standard benchmark (MMLU)
  • their scores on 30 held-out Lumora questions, graded by a judge you've proved you can trust
  • a head-to-head ranking of the systems
  • every result logged, ready for Module 3 to compare against

docs.title: Why this is harder than it sounds
docs.text:
A spam filter outputs "spam" or "not spam", and you compare against labels. An LLM outputs free text, and that breaks the simple recipe:

Challenge Lumora example Many correct answers "12 years", "twelve years" and "The warranty lasts 12 years" are all right Many dimensions Correct? Faithful to the source? Helpful? Safe? In Lumora's tone? Fluent wrong answers "The Vault 10 has 13.5 kWh" reads exactly like a correct answer Prompt sensitivity Changing the prompt format can move benchmark scores by several points Contamination Public benchmark questions leak onto the web and into training data Goodhart's law "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"

No single number captures quality. Good evaluation combines methods, each answering one question, and is honest about each method's error:

Method Question it answers Cost Main weakness Eyeballing Does it work at all? Your time Doesn't scale; fluent errors fool you Benchmarks (MMLU...) How capable is the model in general? Low Not your domain; contamination Reference metrics (exact match, F1) Does the answer match a known answer? Very low Punish paraphrase, reward word overlap LLM-as-a-judge Is this free-text answer correct? Medium Leniency, position and length biases Pairwise + Elo Which system is better overall? Medium Order effects; needs many comparisons Human evaluation Ground truth for all of the above High Slow, expensive; raters disagree too

docs.title: Part A: How capable are the models in general?
Step 1: Look at the answers
docs.text:
Start by reading what the model says. Ask the small model a few Lumora questions with no documents in the prompt (closed-book) and read its answers.

It answers fluently and confidently, and it has never seen a word about Lumora. That's hallucination, and it's why reading answers isn't enough: a confident wrong answer looks just like a right one, and nobody can read 10,000 of them. You need measurements.

▶ Lab: Step 1

Run the setup cells and the eyeballing cell. How many of the answers would you have believed?

The first measurement is the broadest: how capable is each model in general?

docs.title: What MMLU is
docs.text:
MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, Hendrycks et al., 2021) has about 14,000 four-option multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, from elementary maths and astronomy to law and medicine. Random guessing scores 25%. For years it was the headline number for general knowledge and reasoning. Know its limits when you read model cards:

  • Saturation: frontier models score near the top, so differences stop meaning much. Harder successors such as MMLU-Pro exist for this reason.
  • Label errors: a small percentage of questions have wrong or ambiguous answers.
  • Contamination: the questions have been public since 2020 and appear in web crawls.
  • Not your domain: a high MMLU score says nothing about Lumora's warranty.

So in this workshop, MMLU has one specific job: detecting damage. If training on Lumora data in Module 3 hurts the model's general ability, MMLU drops.

docs.title: Zero-shot vs few-shot
docs.text:
Zero-shot gives the model the question alone. Few-shot shows k solved examples first, typically 5. Brown et al. (2020, the GPT-3 paper) showed that models improve markedly from a few examples in the prompt without any training. This is in-context learning. The examples show the format ("answer with a single letter") and prime the task. Small models usually gain the most.

▶ Lab: Exercise 1, build MMLU prompts

Write build_prompt for zero-shot and 5-shot. The check confirms the structure and that no answer leaks into the prompt.

Now you have prompts. The next question is how to read the model's answer reliably.

docs.title: Step 3: Score by log-likelihood
docs.text:
You could let the model write an answer and pick out "The answer is B" with a pattern, but models write "B)", "(B)", "Option B", or explain first and answer last. Parsing is fragile, and random sampling adds noise.

Evaluation harnesses instead end the prompt with Answer: and look at the probability the model gives to each possible next token:

...
C. It would be harder since the truck is lighter on Mars.
D. It would be the same no matter where you are.
Answer:      ->  P(" A") = 0.08   P(" B") = 0.71   P(" C") = 0.05   P(" D") = 0.16   -> predict B

One forward pass per question, no parsing, and the same answer every run.

Why the leading space in ' A'?

Tokenizers usually treat a word and the same word with a space in front as different tokens. After "Answer:" the natural continuation is " B", with a space. The probability of "B" without the space measures something the model rarely writes. Details like this are why different harnesses report slightly different numbers for the same model.

▶ Lab: Exercise 2, write predict_letters

Score each prompt by comparing the next-token probabilities of " A" to " D". Then run MMLU zero-shot and 5-shot for both models and compare.

General ability is measured. But MMLU can't tell you the thing Lumora cares about most.

docs.title: Part B: How much do they know about Lumora?
Step 4: Test Lumora knowledge, closed-book and open-book
docs.text:
Public benchmarks can't tell you whether a model knows your domain. For that you need your own test set. The lab ships one: 30 human-written Lumora questions with reference answers, covering products, warranty, error codes, policies and engineering notes.

Rules for a trustworthy domain test

  1. Held out: never used for training, prompt examples or tuning.
  2. Written independently of the training data, ideally by different people.
  3. Covers the categories you care about, with enough questions in each.
  4. Clear reference answers. Avoid yes/no questions: a model guesses those right 50% of the time.
  5. Versioned, so scores from different months are comparable.

The lab runs three setups:

Setup Prompt contains Measures Small model, closed-book The question What the model knows Large model, closed-book The question Whether a bigger model knows more Large model, open-book The question plus the source document Whether the model can use the knowledge when it has it

Expect both closed-book setups to score low and open-book to score near 100%. Two lessons: a bigger model doesn't know facts it never saw, and the gap between closed-book and open-book is the size of Lumora's knowledge problem. Retrieval (RAG) closes it by putting documents in the prompt at question time; Module 3 closes it by training the knowledge in.

docs.title: A cheap metric first, and why it isn't enough
docs.text:
The cheapest way to grade an answer is to compare it with the reference:

Metric How Fails on Exact match The answer equals the reference (after normalising) Any paraphrase: "twelve years" vs "12 years." Token F1 Word overlap (F-score): the balance of precision and recall Wrong answers that reuse the question's words ROUGE / BLEU Overlap of word sequences The same, plus length effects Embedding similarity Cosine similarity of sentence embeddings "12 years" and "15 years" look almost identical

Token F1 rewarding the wrong answer

Reference: "12 years."

  • Answer A: "The Lumora Vault warranty lasts for 12 years." F1 = 0.40 (correct, but wordy)
  • Answer B: "The Lumora Vault warranty typically lasts 5 years." F1 = 0.20 (wrong, still gets credit)
  • Answer C: "Twelve years." F1 = 0.50 (correct, but "twelve" doesn't match "12")

The correct answers score only 0.4-0.5, and the wrong one gets half as much credit. Reference metrics are fine for short, standard answers such as numbers and names; free-text answers need a grader that understands meaning.

▶ Lab: Step 4

Generate closed-book and open-book answers, compute token F1, and read the answers next to their scores. Does F1 reward the right things?

So you need a grader that understands meaning: another LLM. But a grader you haven't tested is just another source of error.

docs.title: Step 5: Build a judge you can trust
The idea
docs.text:
Use an LLM to grade answers: give it the question, the reference answer and the candidate, and ask "Is the candidate correct?". Zheng et al. (2023) found that a strong judge such as GPT-4 agreed with human preferences about 80% of the time, roughly as often as two humans agree. That made LLM judging the standard way to grade open-ended output at scale.

Setup Judge sees Use when Reference-guided grading Question + reference + candidate You have a correct answer (the Lumora test) Single-answer scoring Question + candidate, with a rubric No reference, e.g. helpfulness Pairwise comparison Question + two candidates Ranking systems (Step 6)

Judges have well-known biases:

Bias What happens Fix Leniency Says "correct" to fluent nonsense, especially small judges Calibrate on human labels (below) Position bias Prefers whichever answer is shown first, or second Judge both orders and average Length bias Prefers longer answers Rubrics that reward concision Self-preference Rates its own model family higher Use a different, stronger judge

docs.title: A judge is a classifier, so test it like one
docs.text:
When the judge says "correct" or "incorrect", it's a classifier, and human labels are the ground truth:

Human: correct Human: incorrect Judge: correct True positive False positive: hallucination accepted Judge: incorrect False negative: correct answer rejected True negative

Two numbers matter most: agreement (how often the judge matches the human) and the false-positive rate (the share of wrong answers the judge accepts). The second is the dangerous one, because it inflates your model's score and hides the hallucinations you're trying to measure.

docs.title: A real example from building this lab
docs.text:
1. Hand-written test cases looked fine. On 30 invented answers, a 1.5B judge agreed with the human labels about 90% of the time.
  2. Real model answers told a different story. On actual closed-book answers from the candidate models, the same judge accepted about half as correct, when a careful human reading found only about 10% were. Real hallucinations are fluent, specific and plausible ("The warranty typically lasts 5 years"). Invented test cases rarely look like that.
  3. The lesson: test the judge on the kind of answers it will actually grade. The lab's calibration set has 155 items, 120 of them real answers from the candidate models, each labelled by a person.

docs.title: Calibrate with the judge's confidence
docs.text:
Instead of trusting the judge's Yes or No, read how confident it is from the probability of its first token:

\[\text{score} = \log P(\text{"Yes"}) - \log P(\text{"No"})\]

A positive score means it leans Yes. Then choose the threshold from the human labels: try every candidate threshold on the calibration questions and keep the one with the best agreement. On ties, choose the stricter threshold, because accepting hallucinations is the costlier mistake.

Never tune and report on the same data. The lab tunes on questions q01-q15 and reports on q16-q30, so no question's answers appear on both sides:

Judge Agreement (tuning set) Agreement (test set) Hallucinations accepted (test set) Naive (threshold 0: trust its Yes/No) 88% 86% 21% Calibrated (threshold about 4.0) 95% 84% 3%

Agreement barely changes, but accepted hallucinations drop from about 1 in 5 to about 1 in 30, and that's what protects your scores. The calibrated judge also does better on the tuning set than on the test set: the threshold slightly overfits the data it was tuned on, which is why you report the test number.

Beyond accuracy: Cohen's kappa

If 90% of answers are wrong, a judge that always says "incorrect" scores 90% agreement while learning nothing. Cohen's kappa corrects for chance agreement: \(\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\), where \(p_o\) is the observed agreement and \(p_e\) the agreement expected by chance. Values above about 0.6 are usually read as substantial agreement. The lab's calibration set is roughly balanced, so accuracy is meaningful there; use kappa when your classes are skewed.

▶ Lab: Exercise 3, calibrate the judge

Write pick_threshold, compare the naive and calibrated judges on the test questions, then grade all three systems with your calibrated judge.

You can now score answers against a reference. But some questions don't have one.

docs.title: Step 6: Rank the systems head to head
Why compare in pairs?
docs.text: For style, helpfulness or chat quality there's no single right answer, and absolute scores drift ("is this a 7 or an 8?"). People and LLM judges are more consistent at relative judgements: "Is A or B better?". Chatbot Arena ranks models this way from millions of votes.

docs.title: The Elo system
docs.text:
Each system has a rating \(R\) (see Elo rating system). Before a comparison, the expected score of A against B is:

\[E_A = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/400}}\]

After it, with actual score \(S_A\) (1 for a win, 0.5 for a tie, 0 for a loss, or any probability in between):

\[R_A' = R_A + K\,(S_A - E_A), \qquad R_B' = R_B - K\,(S_A - E_A)\] Rating gap Expected win rate of the higher-rated system 0 50% 100 64% 200 76% 400 91%

\(K\) (the lab uses 32) sets how far one comparison moves the ratings. What A gains, B loses. An upset moves ratings a lot; an expected result barely moves them.

docs.title: Practical details
docs.text:
• Order: Elo processes comparisons one at a time, so the order changes the final ratings. The lab averages over 50 random orders. Chatbot Arena switched to the Bradley-Terry model, which fits all results at once.
  • Position bias: the lab judges every pair twice, with the answers swapped, and averages. The notebook prints the measured bias; small judges often lean clearly towards one position.
  • Uncertainty: ratings from a few dozen comparisons are noisy. Report confidence intervals (bootstrap: resample the comparisons, recompute, repeat) when systems are close.

▶ Lab: Exercise 4, write elo_expected and elo_update

Pass the unit tests, then run the tournament: every pair of systems on every question, judged in both orders.

docs.title: Is the difference real?
docs.text:
Before you announce a winner, check that the gap isn't noise. With 30 questions, each one is worth 3.3 percentage points. If a model's true accuracy is 50%, the 95% confidence interval on a 30-question test is roughly:

\[\pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.5 \times 0.5}{30}} \approx \pm 18 \text{ points}\]

So "57% vs 50%" on 30 questions is not evidence of a difference. "10% vs 70%" is.

  • Use a few hundred questions before trusting single-digit differences.
  • Compare models on the same questions and look at which ones changed.
  • Generate with temperature 0, as the lab does, or average several runs.
  • Count the judge's error rate as part of the noise.

You now have a lot of numbers. The last step makes sure they're still useful next week.

docs.title: Step 7: Record everything in MLflow
docs.text:
Three weeks from now, nobody will remember which prompt, model version or judge threshold produced "72%". Module 3 needs to compare its trained models against exactly these baselines. MLflow organises results as:

Concept Meaning Lab example Experiment A group of related runs lumora-eval Run One evaluation of one configuration mmlu-Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-5shot Params What you did model, benchmark, k_shot, judge Metrics What happened mmlu_acc, lumora_acc, token_f1, elo Tags Free-form labels tier = free / pro Artifacts Files predictions, plots, the judge prompt

For full reproducibility, also record the model revision (its commit on Hugging Face), the dataset version, prompt templates, seeds and library versions.

▶ Lab: Exercise 5, write log_run

Log every MMLU and Lumora result with its parameters and metrics, then query them back.

▶ Lab: Pro bonus, cross-check with lm-evaluation-harness (Colab Pro)

Your MMLU numbers come from code you wrote. Production teams use standard harnesses so results are comparable across papers. Run the harness and compare its number with yours.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Read answers first, then measure. Fluent doesn't mean correct.
  • Use each method for its own question. MMLU for general ability (and damage), your own test for domain knowledge, a judge for free text, pairwise comparison for overall quality.
  • Test the judge before trusting it, on real answers, and report its error on held-out data.
  • Small test sets are noisy. Don't declare a winner on a few points.
  • Record everything, or you can't compare later.

docs.title: Module 3: Customising LLMs (CPT, SFT, DPO)
docs.text: Time: about 85 minutes, reading and lab together  |  Track: Free (T4), with a Pro bonus

docs.title: The situation
docs.text:
Module 2 set the baseline: on the 30 held-out Lumora questions, the small base model answered about 10% correctly, and most of that was lucky guessing. Lumora's leadership now wants an assistant that does three things:

  1. Knows Lumora's products and policies (knowledge)
  2. Answers questions in a short, support-style format (a skill)
  3. Sounds like Lumora: warm and friendly (behaviour)

Each goal needs a different training technique, and in this module you'll use all three on the data you built in Module 1. You'll train five models and grade them all with Module 2's calibrated judge, so you can see exactly what each technique adds.

docs.title: Why the model needs training
docs.text:
A language model learns one task: predict the next token. Given "The Eiffel Tower is in", it assigns a probability to every token, and training nudges the weights so "Paris" gets more. After trillions of tokens the weights hold a compressed memory of the training text, called parametric knowledge. Three things follow:

  1. The model only knows what was in its training data. No model has ever seen "the Vault 10 has 10.2 kWh of usable capacity".
  2. Not knowing doesn't stop it answering. It was trained to produce plausible text, not to say "I don't know", so it invents a capacity or a warranty term. That's a hallucination.
  3. To change what it knows, you change its weights, or you put the information in front of it when the question is asked.

Module 2 showed the second option works: with the source document in the prompt (open-book), the model scored near 100%. So why train at all?

In the prompt (RAG) In the weights (fine-tuning) How Find relevant documents and paste them into the prompt Train the model on the information Lumora result Open-book: about 100% (Module 2) Closed-book: from about 10% to about 70% (this module) Update a fact Edit the document, instantly Retrain Cost per question Higher: long prompts, plus a search system to run Lower: short prompts Good at Fast-changing facts, citations, large document sets Stable vocabulary, style, behaviour, answer format Weak at Behaviour and style Fresh facts; risk of forgetting other skills

In practice teams combine both

A common pattern: fine-tune for domain language, tone and answer format, and use RAG for facts that change. This module focuses on fine-tuning, and seeing how far closed-book knowledge can go also shows you what RAG buys you.

docs.title: Three goals, three techniques
docs.text:
Continued pretraining (CPT) Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Direct preference optimisation (DPO) Goal Knowledge Skills, answer format Behaviour: style, tone, safety Data Raw domain text (manuals, policies) Prompt and ideal response Prompt, a chosen and a rejected response Learns from Every token Response tokens only The difference between chosen and rejected Lab setup Full fine-tuning, 6 epochs, LR 3e-5 LoRA r=16, 6 epochs, LR 2e-4 LoRA r=16, 3 epochs, LR 5e-5, beta 0.1 Typical failure Forgets general skills Learns the format, invents the facts Over-optimisation: fluent but empty

In production the usual order is CPT, then SFT, then DPO: first know, then do, then behave.

docs.title: Step 1: Measure the baseline
docs.text:
Every trained model is compared with the untouched base model on three measurements:

  • Answers to the 30 held-out Lumora questions, graded by the judge in Step 5
  • Perplexity on held-out Lumora fact sentences: how surprising the facts are to the model
  • MMLU on a small slice: whether training damaged general knowledge

Perplexity is the exponential of the training loss, \(\text{PPL} = e^{\mathcal{L}}\). Roughly, it's how many tokens the model is choosing between at each step: a perplexity of 20 means it's about as unsure as picking from 20 options. The fact sentences are the evaluation questions with their reference answers, which are never trained on.

▶ Lab: Step 1

Run the setup and baseline cells. Note the base model's perplexity and MMLU, and read a few of its answers.

The base model finds Lumora's facts very surprising. The first technique changes that.

docs.title: The objective
docs.text:
CPT uses exactly the objective the model was originally trained with. For a document of tokens \(x_1 \dots x_T\), the loss is the average negative log-probability of each token given everything before it:

\[\mathcal{L}_\text{CPT} = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_1, \dots, x_{t-1})\]

Every token is a training target. When the model reads "The Vault 10 weighs" and the next token is "98", the update makes "98" more likely in that context. Repeat across every sentence for several epochs and the facts become part of the model's memory. Gururangan et al. (2020) showed that continuing pretraining on in-domain text consistently helps.

docs.title: Memorising vs knowing: why paraphrases matter
docs.text:
A model that has seen "The Vault 10 weighs 98 kg" fifty times can recite it, but may still fail "How heavy is the Vault 10?". Allen-Zhu & Li (2023) found that models reliably answer new questions about a fact only when they saw it in several phrasings during training. One phrasing tends to be stored as a string, not as a fact.

That's why the CPT corpus contains each of the 20 Lumora documents plus 2-3 paraphrases written by an LLM (an FAQ version, a training-note version, a plain paragraph). A paraphrase was kept only if every number in the original survived. Even so, a few contain small errors, such as "after purchase" instead of "after delivery": generated data needs the same checks as real data.

docs.title: Full fine-tuning, not LoRA, for CPT
docs.text:
The lab updates all of the model's roughly 494 million parameters (full fine-tuning). When this lab was built, LoRA-based CPT (explained in Step 3) reached about 27% on the Lumora test, while full CPT reached about 50%. That matches published findings: on knowledge-heavy training, LoRA learns substantially less than full fine-tuning (Biderman et al., 2024). It also forgets less, which is the other side of the same trade-off.

How it works: does full fine-tuning fit on a free T4?

Training with the Adam optimiser in fp32 needs about 16 bytes per parameter:

Item Bytes per parameter 0.5B model Weights (fp32) 4 2 GB Gradients 4 2 GB Adam first moment (m) 4 2 GB Adam second moment (v) 4 2 GB Total, before activations 16 about 8 GB

A T4 has 16 GB, so a 0.5B model fits, but activations need room too: over Qwen's 151,000-token vocabulary, the output layer alone needs 1-2 GB per batch of 4. So on GPUs the lab uses 8-bit Adam, which shrinks the two moment buffers from 8 to 2 bytes per parameter. A 1.5B model (Pro track) would need about 24 GB, so it also uses gradient checkpointing (recomputing activations during the backward pass instead of storing them). A 7B model would need about 112 GB, which is why LoRA exists.

docs.title: Catastrophic forgetting
docs.text: Every update that makes Lumora's facts more likely also moves weights that encoded other things. Push hard on a tiny corpus for many epochs and general ability degrades: catastrophic forgetting. The lab watches for it with the MMLU slice. Production recipes limit it by mixing in 10-30% general text ("replay"), using a lower learning rate and fewer epochs, and stopping early if a general benchmark drops.

docs.title: Data format and pitfalls
docs.text:
One document per row, with the end-of-text token appended so the model learns where documents stop:

{"text": "The Lumora Vault 10 is a wall-mounted home battery with 10.2 kWh of usable capacity. ... <|im_end|>"}

CPT pitfalls

  • Learning rate too high for full fine-tuning (for example 2e-4, a LoRA rate): the loss spikes and general ability collapses. Use about 1e-5 to 5e-5.
  • Too few epochs on a tiny corpus: the facts never stick. The lab uses 6 epochs over 68 texts.
  • Too many epochs: the training loss approaches 0 and the model recites documents when asked anything.

▶ Lab: Exercise 1, prepare the CPT data and training config

Add end-of-text tokens, choose a learning rate suited to full fine-tuning, and train. The check requires perplexity on the held-out facts to drop by at least 30%.

After CPT the model knows more, but it was trained to continue documents. Ask it a question and it may carry on writing a manual page. That's the next problem.

docs.title: Part B: Teach it to answer
What SFT is for
docs.text: SFT shows the model many examples of input and desired output, so it learns a behaviour: here, answering a support question in one short, accurate sentence. The training data is the Q&A set from Module 1.

docs.title: The objective, and loss masking
docs.text:
The loss has the same form as CPT, but only the response tokens count:

\[\mathcal{L}_\text{SFT} = -\frac{1}{|R|}\sum_{t \in R} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})\]

where \(R\) is the set of positions in the assistant's reply. The prompt is still read as context, but its tokens are masked (their labels set to -100) so they contribute nothing to the update:

Tokens <system> You are Lumora's support assistant... <user> How long is the Vault warranty? <assistant> 12 years. <end> In the loss? no (masked) no (masked) yes

Without masking, part of the training effort goes into learning to write questions and system prompts. In TRL you get masking by giving the data in prompt/completion format:

{
  "prompt": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are Lumora Energy's support assistant. Answer in one short sentence."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What does error code E-317 indicate?"}
  ],
  "completion": [
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "The Bridge has lost its internet connection for more than 72 hours."}
  ]
}
What is a chat template?

Instruct models are trained with special tokens that mark who is speaking. Qwen2.5, for example, wraps each turn in <|im_start|>role ... <|im_end|>. The chat template (stored with the tokenizer) turns a list of messages into that exact string. Always use the model's own template, in training and at inference: a mismatch is one of the most common reasons a fine-tuned model behaves strangely. Read more in the Hugging Face chat templates guide.

docs.title: Quality beats quantity
docs.text: The LIMA study (Zhou et al., 2023) fine-tuned a 65B model on just 1,000 carefully chosen examples and got a strong assistant: evidence that SFT mainly teaches format and behaviour, not new knowledge. You'll see the same in Step 5.

docs.title: Decontamination: keep the test out of training
docs.text:
The Q&A pairs were generated from the same 20 documents the test questions were written from, so some are near-copies of test questions:

Training question (generated) Test question (held out) "What is the usable capacity of the Lumora Vault 10?" "What is the usable capacity of the Lumora Vault 10?" "How many Vault 15 units can be connected to a single Bridge inverter?" "What is the maximum number of Vault 15 units on a single Bridge inverter?"

Training on these would inflate the score without teaching anything, like giving students the exam to study. The lab compares content words (what's left after removing "the", "what", "is" and so on) using Jaccard similarity, the same measure Module 1 used for deduplication:

\[J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\]

Any training question with \(J \ge 0.6\) against a test question is dropped; with the shipped data that removes 13 of 101 pairs. At internet scale the same problem is called benchmark contamination.

docs.title: LoRA: training a small fraction of the parameters
docs.text:
SFT here uses LoRA rather than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning updates every weight matrix \(W\). Hu et al. (2021) observed that the change needed during fine-tuning, \(\Delta W\), can usually be approximated by the product of two thin matrices. LoRA freezes \(W\) and learns only those:

\[W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\; r \ll \min(d, k)\]
  • \(r\), the rank, controls capacity. The lab uses 16.
  • \(\alpha\) is a scaling factor; the lab uses \(\alpha = 2r = 32\), a common default.
  • \(B\) starts at zero, so before training the model is exactly the original.
  • After training, \(BA\) can be merged into \(W\), so there's no extra cost at inference.
How it works: how big is a LoRA adapter?

For a matrix of shape \(d \times k\), the adapter adds \(r(d + k)\) parameters. For Qwen2.5-0.5B (hidden size 896, MLP size 4864, 24 layers) with \(r = 16\) on all seven projection matrices:

Matrix Shape LoRA params, r(d+k) q_proj, o_proj 896 x 896 28,672 each k_proj, v_proj 896 x 128 16,384 each gate_proj, up_proj 896 x 4864 92,160 each down_proj 4864 x 896 92,160 Per layer 366,592 24 layers about 8.8M, under 2% of 494M

The optimiser only tracks those 8.8M parameters, so training needs a fraction of the memory. QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) also stores the frozen model in 4-bit, which is how people fine-tune 7-8B models on one consumer GPU.

Transformer blocks have attention projections (q, k, v, o) and MLP projections (gate, up, down). Facts seem to be stored largely in the MLP layers, and adapting only q and v, as the original LoRA paper did, is noticeably weaker. The lab adapts all seven, the modern default.

LoRA Full fine-tuning Trainable parameters about 1-2% 100% Memory Low About 16 bytes per parameter Learns new facts Weakly Well Learns format and style Well Well Forgets general skills Less More Storage A few MB per adapter A full copy per variant Lab use SFT, DPO CPT

Rule of thumb: LoRA when you're changing how the model behaves; full fine-tuning when you're changing what it knows.

▶ Lab: Exercise 2, prepare the SFT data and LoRA config

Convert the Q&A pairs to prompt/completion format, drop contaminated pairs, and target LoRA at all seven projections. Then train two models: SFT on the base model, and SFT on the CPT model.

The model now knows Lumora's facts and answers like support staff. The last goal is how it sounds.

docs.title: Part C: Teach it Lumora's voice
Step 4: Give it Lumora's voice with DPO
Why preferences?
docs.text: Some goals have no single correct answer. What's the ideal friendly reply to "My package hasn't arrived"? There are thousands. But people find it easy to compare two replies and say which is better. Preference data captures that: for each prompt, a chosen reply and a rejected one.

docs.title: From RLHF to DPO
docs.text: The classic recipe, RLHF (used for InstructGPT, Ouyang et al., 2022), has three stages: collect preference pairs, train a separate reward model to score replies as people would, then optimise the LLM with reinforcement learning to maximise that reward without drifting too far from the original. It works, but it means training several models and is notoriously finicky. DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) showed the same goal can be reached directly from the preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss: no reward model and no reinforcement learning.

docs.title: The DPO loss, unpacked
docs.text:
For a prompt \(x\) with chosen reply \(y_w\) and rejected reply \(y_l\):

\[\mathcal{L}_\text{DPO} = -\log \sigma\Big(\beta\big[\underbrace{\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_w|x)}}_{\text{chosen: how much more likely than before}} - \underbrace{\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_l|x)}}_{\text{rejected: how much more likely than before}}\big]\Big)\]

In words:

  • \(\pi_\theta\) is the model being trained; \(\pi_\text{ref}\) is a frozen copy of where it started.
  • Each log-ratio measures how much the model has changed its opinion of a reply since training began.
  • The loss is low when the model has raised the chosen reply more than the rejected one.
  • \(\sigma\) is the sigmoid, so the loss works like logistic regression on "is chosen preferred?"
  • \(\beta\) sets how far the model is allowed to drift from the reference. A small \(\beta\) (0.05) allows big changes; a large one (0.5) keeps it close. 0.1 is a common default.

With LoRA you don't need a second model in memory: the reference is the same network with the adapter switched off.

docs.title: Building the preference pairs, and the trap
docs.text:
The lab asks the 1.5B model to answer each everyday prompt twice: once told to be "warm, casual, use contractions" (chosen) and once told to be "formal, impersonal, no contractions" (rejected).

{
  "prompt":   [{"role": "user", "content": "How do I reset my password?"}],
  "chosen":   [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Hey there! Just hit the \"Forgot Password\" link and follow the steps. If that doesn't work, support's happy to help!"}],
  "rejected": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "To reset your password, please navigate to the login page and select the \"Forgot Password\" option. Further assistance is available from customer support."}]
}

Don't leak the style instruction

The instruction used to generate the chosen reply ("reply casually...") must not be in the training prompt. If it is, the model learns "when told to be casual, be casual", which it could already do. At inference nobody adds that instruction, so the style never appears. The lab's starter code makes exactly this mistake on purpose, and the check catches it.

docs.title: Reading the training logs
docs.text:
Metric Meaning Healthy pattern rewards/chosen \(\beta \times\) log-ratio for chosen replies Stays near 0 or rises rewards/rejected The same for rejected replies Falls (becomes negative) rewards/margins chosen minus rejected Grows steadily rewards/accuracies Share of pairs where chosen beats rejected Rises towards 0.8-1.0

Chosen rewards can go down too

It's common for both rewards to fall, with rejected falling much faster. The margin grows, so the loss looks fine, but the model has made the chosen replies less likely in absolute terms. This "likelihood displacement" is a known DPO quirk, and one reason to always read actual replies, not just metrics.

docs.title: Over-optimisation
docs.text:
Push too hard and DPO games its own signal. At a 4x higher learning rate (2e-4) the lab's model reached even better reward metrics, and its replies collapsed into empty cheerfulness:

"Hey there! Here's some fun ideas!"

It found that exclamation marks and contractions were what separated chosen from rejected, and maximised those at the expense of helpfulness. Any proxy metric can be gamed. Defences: a sensible \(\beta\) and learning rate, fewer epochs, and evaluating helpfulness alongside style. You'll meet this again in Module 5.

Beyond DPO: the alignment family Method Idea RLHF / PPO Reward model plus reinforcement learning. Most flexible, most complex DPO Direct optimisation on preference pairs (this lab) IPO Adds regularisation against overfitting to preferences KTO Needs only a "good" or "bad" label per reply, not pairs ORPO Combines SFT and preference optimisation in one stage, no reference model SimPO Reference-free, length-normalised reward

NeMo-RL and TRL implement several of these. The data and evaluation discipline is the same.

▶ Lab: Exercise 3, build the preference pairs

Write to_preference without leaking the style instruction, train with DPO, and watch the reward metrics. The check requires reward accuracy of at least 80% and a style shift on prompts the model never saw. Optionally, re-run with learning rate 2e-4 and read what happens.

You now have five models. Time to find out what each technique really did.

docs.title: Step 5: Grade everything with Module 2's judge
docs.text:
The notebook recalibrates Module 2's judge (same method, same data) and grades all five models' answers. Results from our reference run (yours will vary by a few points):

Model Lumora accuracy Fact perplexity MMLU What happened base 10% 86 68% Doesn't know Lumora sft 20% 50 70% Perfect one-sentence format, invented facts cpt 50% 15 70% Knows the facts, but answers can ramble cpt+sft 70% 11 70% Knowledge plus the answer format dpo 3% 86 68% Casual tone, no Lumora knowledge: it chats instead of stating facts

Three lessons:

  1. SFT alone doesn't add knowledge. About 90 Q&A pairs can't teach 20 documents' worth of facts. SFT teaches how to answer, and the model fills that shape with whatever it knows. With CPT first, it knows the right things.
  2. Perplexity on held-out facts fell from 86 to 11, even though the model never saw those exact sentences: the knowledge generalised.
  3. MMLU didn't move on the 50-question slice, so there's no measurable forgetting at this scale. Longer training or a bigger corpus can cost general knowledge, so always check.

The DPO model also shows why techniques stack: it learned the voice (its casualness score on unseen prompts rose from 0.17 to 0.77) but, trained on the base model, it knows nothing about Lumora.

docs.title: The hyperparameters, and why
docs.text:
CPT SFT DPO Method Full fine-tuning LoRA r=16, alpha=32 LoRA r=16, alpha=32 Learning rate 3e-5 2e-4 5e-5 Epochs 6 6 3 Batch size 8 8 4 x 2 accumulation Schedule Cosine, 2 warm-up steps Cosine Cosine Why A small learning rate protects general ability; several epochs because the corpus is tiny LoRA tolerates a higher rate; repeated passes fix the format A gentle rate avoids over-optimisation; beta 0.1 is the standard anchor

Learning rates differ by about 10x between full fine-tuning and LoRA because LoRA's update starts at zero and is scaled by \(\alpha / r\). Copying a LoRA learning rate into a full fine-tune is one of the most common ways to wreck a model.

docs.title: Module result
docs.text: The notebook logs every model to MLflow and saves results.json. You now have an assistant that knows Lumora and answers like support. Module 4 asks the next question: how to make a model like this small and fast enough to deploy.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• CPT adds knowledge, SFT adds skills, DPO shapes behaviour. Use the right tool for the goal, and stack them: CPT, then SFT, then DPO.
  • LoRA changes behaviour cheaply; full fine-tuning changes knowledge.
  • Keep the test out of training, or your scores mean nothing.
  • Read the outputs, not just the metrics. Over-optimised DPO and likelihood displacement both look fine on the reward curves.
  • Check general ability after every stage.

docs.title: Module 4: Optimising LLMs for deployment
docs.text: Time: about 75 minutes, reading and lab together  |  Track: Free (T4), with a Pro bonus

docs.title: The situation
docs.text:
Module 3 produced an assistant that knows Lumora and answers like support staff. Now Lumora's finance team has a question: what will it cost to run? Every customer question means paying for every token the model generates, for every customer, for as long as the assistant is live.

They want it smaller and faster, without it getting noticeably worse. In this module you'll try the three main compression techniques and measure exactly what each one costs:

  1. Quantization: store each weight in fewer bits
  2. Pruning: delete whole layers
  3. Distillation: let the original model repair the pruned one

Then you'll put the results side by side and decide which version Lumora should ship.

To keep the measurements clean, the lab compresses the base student model (Qwen2.5-0.5B on the free track) and measures perplexity on held-out Wikipedia text (general language ability; lower is better), an MMLU slice (knowledge), speed and size. The same techniques apply unchanged to the model you trained in Module 3.

docs.title: Why optimise?
docs.text:
Goal Why it matters Memory Fit on a cheaper GPU, or serve more customers per GPU Latency Time to first token and time per token decide how responsive it feels Throughput Tokens per second across all customers decides the cost per request Energy and cost Fewer GPU-hours for the same traffic

The constraint: accuracy must stay acceptable on the tasks you care about. Every technique here trades some accuracy for efficiency, and the job is to measure that trade-off.

docs.title: Where inference time goes
docs.text:
Generating text has two phases:

  1. Prefill: the whole prompt is processed at once. This keeps the GPU's maths units busy (compute-bound).
  2. Decode: tokens are generated one at a time. For each new token the GPU must read every weight from memory, but does relatively little maths with it (memory-bandwidth-bound).

For a 7B model in FP16 (14 GB), each new token means reading 14 GB of weights. A GPU with about 1 TB/s of memory bandwidth can therefore manage at most about 70 tokens per second for one user, however fast its maths units are. Halve the bytes per weight and you roughly double that limit. That's why quantization is the first optimisation almost everyone applies.

The KV cache: the other big memory user

During generation the model stores each past token's attention keys and values so it doesn't recompute them. That cache grows with conversation length and the number of conversations served at once:

\[\text{KV bytes} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{kv\_heads} \times \text{head\_dim} \times \text{tokens} \times \text{batch} \times \text{bytes per value}\]

For Qwen2.5-0.5B (24 layers, 2 KV heads of dimension 64) in FP16 that's about 12 KB per token, so 32 conversations of 4,000 tokens each need about 1.5 GB. For large models with long contexts the KV cache can be bigger than the weights. It can be quantized too (for example an FP8 KV cache), and grouped-query attention (GQA, used by Qwen and Llama) exists to shrink it.
